knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)

This document is the R counterpart of the Python notebook
[Part 01 - Collecting Data at Scale](../../Notebooks/Part%2001%20-%20Collecting%20Data%20at%20Scale/Part%2001%20-%20Collecting%20Data%20at%20Scale.ipynb).
It builds the same documented archive of one account's posts, follows,
and followers — and teaches the same craft of collecting it responsibly
— using [bskyr](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/) and the tidyverse.

## Background

Part 00 made single API calls and looked at the first page of results.
Real research needs collections that are *complete where completeness is
feasible and deliberately bounded where it is not*: every account our
case study follows, but only a defensible sample of its 1.3 million
followers. Getting from one page to an archive raises the questions this
part answers: how endpoints paginate, how fast we may call them, how to
flatten nested API responses into tidy data frames, and how to store an
archive so that our future selves — and other researchers — can use it.

### Learning objectives

* Define a sampling frame before collecting anything.
* Explain cursor-based pagination, and use bskyr's automatic paging.
* Wrap API calls in retry logic with exponential backoff.
* Flatten nested responses into tidy tibbles.
* Persist archives to disk with collection metadata for reproducibility.

## Setup

Alongside the core trio from Part 00, this part adds **lubridate**, the
tidyverse's package for parsing and manipulating dates and times — API
timestamps arrive as ISO-8601 strings, and lubridate turns them into
objects we can sort, bin, and plot:

```{r libraries}
library(bskyr)
library(tidyverse)
library(jsonlite)
library(lubridate)
```

As in every part of this series, the shared helper `bsky_client.R` looks
for credentials (an `atproto.json` file or bskyr's environment
variables), authenticates if it finds them, and sets `bsky_authed`. The
`knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = bsky_authed)` line then makes that flag the
default for the whole document: with credentials every chunk runs;
without them the document still knits, but the API chunks are skipped.

```{r connect}
source("bsky_client.R")
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = bsky_authed)
```

## 1. Before you collect: define a sampling frame

A *sampling frame* is the explicit list of units your data could possibly
contain. Ours is one account, collected three ways: a census of the
accounts it follows, the most recent slice of its posts, and a small
sample of its most recent followers. Checking the profile first tells
us how much work each would be:

```{r frame}
HANDLE <- "nytimes.com"

profile <- bs_get_profile(HANDLE)

profile |>
  select(handle, did, created_at, posts_count, follows_count, followers_count)
```

Each paginated endpoint returns at most 100 records per request, so the
counters above translate directly into a request budget. The
`pivot_longer()` call below reshapes the three counter columns into
rows — one row per collection — so we can compute the budget for all
three with a single `mutate()`:

```{r budget}
PAGE_SIZE <- 100

profile |>
  select(posts_count, follows_count, followers_count) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "collection", values_to = "records") |>
  mutate(requests_needed = ceiling(records / PAGE_SIZE))
```

This arithmetic is the lesson. The follows list is two requests. The
posts are a few hundred. The followers of a major newsroom are over a
million records — more than *ten thousand* requests: hours of collection
that would strain the API and hand us a giant file of third parties we
have no question about. Always do this arithmetic *before* you start
collecting, and let it talk you out of "collect everything."

## 2. The anatomy of a paginated endpoint

Ask for one page of the author feed and bskyr returns a tibble of (up to)
100 posts, with the *cursor* — an opaque bookmark marking where the next
page begins — stored as an attribute:

```{r page1}
page1 <- bs_get_author_feed(HANDLE, limit = 100)

nrow(page1)
attr(page1, "cursor")$cursor
```

Passing that cursor back retrieves the next page; the two pages should
not overlap:

```{r page2}
page2 <- bs_get_author_feed(HANDLE, limit = 100,
                            cursor = attr(page1, "cursor")$cursor)

length(intersect(page1$uri, page2$uri))
```

Zero overlap: page 2 picks up exactly where page 1 left off. Walking
cursors until the server stops returning one is all "collecting at
scale" means.

## 3. A reusable collection loop

In the Python series we wrote `fetch_all_pages()` by hand. bskyr builds
the same loop into every paginated function: ask for `limit > 100` and it
issues ceiling(limit/100) requests behind the scenes, following cursors
until the limit — or the end of the data — is reached.

One choice deserves explaining. Normally bskyr *cleans* each response
into a tidy tibble, one row per post. That is convenient, but it costs
time per post: roughly 20–90 milliseconds, depending on your bskyr
version, so 10,000 posts would take between 3 and 15 minutes to clean.
For a collection this size we ask for the **raw pages** instead
(`clean = FALSE`) and pull out only the fields we need ourselves in
Section 5. That's faster, and it's data minimization too. Smaller
collections can use the tidy version, as Part 00 did.

One more thing to know: bskyr fetches the pages back to back, without
the polite pause our Python loop adds. At about 100 requests that's
fine; for much larger crawls, loop over cursors yourself and add
`Sys.sleep(0.1)` between pages.

The three limits mirror the Python notebook's `max_pages` caps, written
as record counts: 100 pages of posts, a follows limit with plenty of
headroom (so that list is a census), and 20 pages of followers:

```{r collect-all}
POSTS_LIMIT     <- 10000   # Python: max_pages = 100
FOLLOWS_LIMIT   <- 4000    # Python: max_pages = 40; a census, the list is far shorter
FOLLOWERS_LIMIT <- 2000    # Python: max_pages = 20

posts_pages <- bs_get_author_feed(HANDLE, limit = POSTS_LIMIT, clean = FALSE)
follows     <- bs_get_follows(HANDLE, limit = FOLLOWS_LIMIT)
followers   <- bs_get_followers(HANDLE, limit = FOLLOWERS_LIMIT)

items <- list_flatten(map(posts_pages, "feed"))   # every page's items, in order

c(feed_items = length(items), follows = nrow(follows), followers = nrow(followers))
```

Note what the caps did. The follows list (small enough to take in
full) came back *complete*. The posts came back capped at 10,000 — the most
recent slice of a longer history. And the followers stopped at 2,000 of
more than a million: a deliberate **sample of the most recent
followers**, because no analysis below needs all of them. A `limit` is a
budget and a design decision at once; never write a loop whose only
stopping condition is "the API ran out of data."

## 4. Rate limits, polite clients, and exponential backoff

Why all this fuss about caps and pauses? Because APIs meter access.
Bluesky's [documented rate limits](https://bsky.network/docs/advanced-guides/rate-limits)
have two layers:

* **Per-IP request limit:** at most **3,000 requests per 5-minute
  window** to a PDS host. At a polite pace this is hard to hit with one
  document, but a parallelized crawler hits it fast.
* **Write limits in "points":** creating a record costs 3 points,
  updating 2, deleting 1, with budgets of **5,000 points per hour** and
  **35,000 per day** per account, roughly 1,666 new posts, likes or
  follows per hour. These exist to stop spam and matter for the bots of
  Part 10, not for read-only collection.

There are also per-account session limits (for example, 30 new sessions
per 5 minutes), which is one reason `bsky_client.R` logs in once and
bskyr reuses the session.

How do you know where you stand? Servers tell you, in **`RateLimit-*`
HTTP response headers** attached to every response. One subtlety of
Bluesky's architecture: these headers come from **PDS hosts** (personal
data servers, like `bsky.social`, which enforce the limits), not from
the public AppView. We can read them with a single raw
[httr2](https://httr2.r-lib.org/) request to a harmless PDS endpoint,
`com.atproto.server.describeServer`:

```{r rate-headers}
resp <- httr2::request("https://bsky.social/xrpc/com.atproto.server.describeServer") |>
  httr2::req_perform()

httr2::resp_headers(resp)[c("ratelimit-limit", "ratelimit-remaining",
                            "ratelimit-reset", "ratelimit-policy")]
```

Reading these from the top: this IP may make `ratelimit-limit` requests
per window (`ratelimit-policy` spells out the window, `w=300` seconds),
it has `ratelimit-remaining` requests left, and the window resets at
`ratelimit-reset`, a Unix timestamp. Convert it to a readable time with
`as_datetime(as.numeric(...))` from lubridate if you want to know when a
big collection can safely start.

### Handling 429s with exponential backoff

If you exhaust the budget anyway, the server answers **HTTP status 429
("Too Many Requests")**, with the error name `RateLimitExceeded`. A 429
is not a failure to be caught and ignored: it is the server telling you
to slow down, and the correct response is to **wait and retry, waiting
longer after each successive failure**.

That strategy is called **exponential backoff**: wait 1 second, then 2,
then 4, 8, 16, ..., usually with a dash of random "jitter" so that many
clients rate-limited at the same moment don't all retry in synchrony and
re-overload the server. The wrapper below uses R's `tryCatch()`, which
runs a piece of code and, instead of crashing on an error, hands the
error to us as an object we can inspect. Two details matter:

* httr2, the HTTP engine inside bskyr, gives every HTTP error a class
  naming its status, so a rate limit is an error of class
  `httr2_http_429`. We also check the message for `RateLimitExceeded`.
* Anything that *isn't* a rate limit is re-raised immediately, because
  retrying a typo'd handle five times helps no one. This matches the
  Python version's `call_with_backoff`.

```{r backoff}
is_rate_limit_error <- function(e) {
  inherits(e, "httr2_http_429") || grepl("RateLimitExceeded|429", conditionMessage(e))
}

call_with_backoff <- function(fun, ..., max_tries = 5, base_wait = 1) {
  for (attempt in seq_len(max_tries)) {
    result <- tryCatch(fun(...), error = function(e) e)
    if (!inherits(result, "error")) {
      return(result)
    }
    if (!is_rate_limit_error(result) || attempt == max_tries) {
      stop(result)   # not a rate limit, or out of retries: give up now
    }
    wait <- base_wait * 2^(attempt - 1) + runif(1, 0, 0.5)   # 1, 2, 4, ... s plus jitter
    message("Rate limited; retrying in ", round(wait, 1), "s")
    Sys.sleep(wait)
  }
}

bsky_profile <- call_with_backoff(bs_get_profile, "bsky.app")
bsky_profile$followers_count
```

In practice you will rarely see the wrapper retry: at our pace the
budget is generous. It is a seatbelt, and Exercise 6 shows how to watch
it work without sending a single real request.

(Under the hood, bskyr's HTTP engine [httr2](https://httr2.r-lib.org/)
can also retry transparently via `req_retry()` — worth knowing when you
write raw XRPC requests, as later parts do.)

### Doing more with fewer requests

The cheapest request is the one you never make. [`bs_get_profile()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_profile.html)
accepts up to 25 actors per call, so hydrating accounts in batches cuts
your request count 25-fold:

```{r batch}
sample_dids <- head(follows$did, 25)

batch <- bs_get_profile(sample_dids)

batch |> select(handle, followers_count, posts_count) |> head(3)
```

## 5. Flattening nested models into tidy data frames

Each raw feed item is a nested list, shaped exactly like the API's JSON:

* `item$post` is the post as the AppView presents it: `uri`, `cid`,
  `author`, and the engagement counters (`likeCount`, `repostCount`, ...);
* `item$post$record` is what the author's app wrote: `text`,
  `createdAt`, `langs`, and a `reply` field if the post is a reply;
* `item$reason`, if present, says *why* the item is in the feed.

We flatten that into one row per post, one column per field. `map_chr()`
walks the list of items and pulls out one value from each.

Two defensive moves here deserve explanation, because you will reuse
them constantly:

* **Missing fields get a default.** `%||%` means "use the left side
  unless it is `NULL`, then the right". A post without a field yields
  `NA` instead of an error.
* **Check what a field says, not just whether it exists.** A repost has
  a `reason` of type `#reasonRepost`. A *pinned* post also has a
  `reason` (type `#reasonPin`), so testing only "does it have a reason?"
  would wrongly throw away the account's pinned post. Bugs like that fail
  silently: the code runs, and the data is quietly wrong.

```{r flatten}
reason_type <- map_chr(items, \(i) i$reason$`$type` %||% NA_character_)

posts <- tibble(
  uri          = map_chr(items, \(i) i$post$uri),
  cid          = map_chr(items, \(i) i$post$cid),
  created_at   = ymd_hms(map_chr(items, \(i) i$post$record$createdAt %||% NA_character_),
                         quiet = TRUE),
  text         = map_chr(items, \(i) i$post$record$text %||% NA_character_),
  is_reply     = map_lgl(items, \(i) !is.null(i$post$record$reply)),
  like_count   = map_int(items, \(i) i$post$likeCount %||% NA_integer_),
  repost_count = map_int(items, \(i) i$post$repostCount %||% NA_integer_),
  reply_count  = map_int(items, \(i) i$post$replyCount %||% NA_integer_),
  quote_count  = map_int(items, \(i) i$post$quoteCount %||% NA_integer_),
  langs        = map_chr(items, \(i) paste(unlist(i$post$record$langs), collapse = ",")),
  has_embed    = map_lgl(items, \(i) !is.null(i$post$embed))
) |>
  filter(is.na(reason_type) | !endsWith(reason_type, "#reasonRepost")) |>  # drop reposts
  arrange(created_at)

c(feed_items = length(items), reposts_dropped = length(items) - nrow(posts))
glimpse(posts)
```

When you work with bskyr's *tidy* tibbles instead, the same information
lives in columns whose names are easy to get wrong. For example, the
repost marker is called `` reason_$type ``, not `reason_type`. The
series' helper file `bsky_client.R` provides `is_repost()` and
`is_reply()`, which later parts use and which are tested against the raw
API data.

One row per post, one column per feature, timestamps parsed — the *tidy
data* shape every later part consumes.

## 6. Persisting archives: CSV, RDS, and metadata

Collection is slow and the network changes under you, so collect once and
analyze from disk. CSV travels everywhere; RDS preserves R types exactly
(the Python series uses Parquet for the same reason):

```{r persist}
dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)

write_csv(posts, "data/posts.csv")
saveRDS(posts, "data/posts.rds")
write_csv(select(follows, did, handle, display_name), "data/follows.csv")
write_csv(select(followers, did, handle, display_name), "data/followers.csv")

file.size(c("data/posts.csv", "data/posts.rds")) / 1024
```

### Recording collection metadata

Data files alone are not an archive. Six months from now (or for the
colleague reproducing your study), the crucial questions will be: *when*
was this collected, *from where*, *with what parameters*, and *what
exactly is in it?* The answers should travel with the data, so we write
them into a small JSON file alongside the archives, the seed of a real
[data management plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_management_plan).

Two fields deserve attention: `limit` and `truncated`. `truncated` is
`TRUE` when a collection stopped at its limit with records still
remaining. That single flag is the difference between "all of this
account's follows" and "the most recent slice of its followers", and a
reader of the archive should never have to guess which one they have.
For the raw post pages the last page's cursor tells us directly. For
bskyr's tidy tibbles, the `cursor` attribute holds the cursors of the
pages that came back *with* one (the last page of a complete list has
none). If every page bskyr requested, one per 100 records of the limit,
carried a cursor, the server still had more to give. (Counting rows
would not work: pages often hold slightly fewer than 100 accounts,
because the AppView drops deactivated and blocked accounts after fetching
a page, so a capped collection can come back under its limit.)

```{r metadata}
posts_truncated <- !is.null(tail(posts_pages, 1)[[1]]$cursor)   # the server had more pages
hit_limit <- function(x, limit) length(attr(x, "cursor")) >= ceiling(limit / 100)

metadata <- list(
  account = list(handle = HANDLE, did = profile$did),
  collected_at_utc = format(now("UTC"), "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"),
  bskyr_version = as.character(packageVersion("bskyr")),
  collections = list(
    posts = list(endpoint = "app.bsky.feed.getAuthorFeed",
                 limit = POSTS_LIMIT, truncated = posts_truncated,
                 n_records = nrow(posts),
                 notes = "Original posts only; reposts excluded."),
    follows = list(endpoint = "app.bsky.graph.getFollows",
                   limit = FOLLOWS_LIMIT, truncated = hit_limit(follows, FOLLOWS_LIMIT),
                   n_records = nrow(follows)),
    followers = list(endpoint = "app.bsky.graph.getFollowers",
                     limit = FOLLOWERS_LIMIT, truncated = hit_limit(followers, FOLLOWERS_LIMIT),
                     n_records = nrow(followers))
  )
)

write_json(metadata, "data/collection_metadata.json",
           pretty = TRUE, auto_unbox = TRUE)

map_lgl(metadata$collections, "truncated")   # which collections are capped slices
```

### Proving the round trip

```{r roundtrip}
reloaded <- readRDS("data/posts.rds")

identical(reloaded, posts)
```

## 7. A first look at the archive

The payoff: months of posting history, summarized in a few lines of
dplyr and ggplot2. We print the slice's date range first, because "the
most recent 10,000 feed items" covers a different calendar window for
every account. `floor_date()` rounds each timestamp down to the
first of its month, and `count()` tallies posts per month — the
month-binning pattern that Part 05 builds a whole time-series toolkit
on:

```{r posts-per-month, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
range(posts$created_at)

posts |>
  count(month = floor_date(created_at, "month")) |>
  ggplot(aes(month, n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Month", y = "Posts",
       title = paste0("Posts per month by @", HANDLE)) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Two things to read off this chart. First, the date range printed above:
for an account that posts dozens of times a day, 10,000 feed items reach
back only a matter of months, so this archive says nothing about the
account's early years on Bluesky. That is the cost of a capped slice,
and it is why Part 05, which needs a fixed date in the past, analyzes a
committed archive instead. Second, the shape: a newsroom posts at a
steady, scheduled cadence, so the full months look broadly similar. The
first and last bars are short because they are **partial months** (the
slice begins partway through one month and ends today), not because
posting dropped. Misreading a partial bin as a decline is one of the
most common mistakes in time-series work, and Part 05 returns to it.

```{r engagement-summary}
posts |>
  summarise(
    share_replies = mean(is_reply),
    share_embeds  = mean(has_embed),
    median_likes  = median(like_count, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_likes     = max(like_count, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

Finally, a simple network question as a teaser for Part 03: how
**reciprocal** is this account's neighborhood? Of the accounts the Times
follows, how many follow it back? Both tables key on DIDs, so the
tempting first attempt is `intersect()`: any DID in both the follows
list and the followers list is a *mutual* follow. Let's try it, and also
compute how much of the full follower list our sample covers:

```{r mutuals}
mutuals <- intersect(follows$did, followers$did)

tibble(
  follows = nrow(follows),
  followers_sampled = nrow(followers),
  followers_total = profile$followers_count,
  share_of_followers_sampled = nrow(followers) / profile$followers_count,
  mutuals_by_intersection = length(mutuals)
) |>
  glimpse()   # one line per column, so nothing is cut off
```

Look at `share_of_followers_sampled` before you look at the mutuals
count. Our follower sample is the **most recent** slice of a list with
over a million entries, a small fraction of a percent of it. An account
the Times followed back in 2023 almost certainly followed the Times long
before the accounts in our slice did, so it sits deep in the part of the
list we never collected. The intersection can only find mutuals among
the newest followers, so its count is mostly a statement about our
sampling design, not about reciprocity. A general trap: **a set
operation between a census and a convenience sample measures the
sample, not the population.**

The fix is to ask the question directly. The
[`app.bsky.graph.getRelationships`](https://endpoints.bsky.app/#bluesky-app/tag/appbskygraph/GET/xrpc/app.bsky.graph.getRelationships)
endpoint takes one `actor` and a list of `others`, and for each pair
reports whether the actor follows them (`following`) and whether they
follow the actor (`followed_by`), as the AT-URIs of the follow records
or `NA`. bskyr wraps it as [`bs_get_relationships()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_relationships.html), which sends the
`others` in batches of 30 (the endpoint's maximum per request), so for a
follows list of this size it makes only a handful of requests:

```{r relationships}
relationships <- call_with_backoff(bs_get_relationships, profile$did, follows$did)

# Accounts that no longer exist come back without the followed_by field
checked <- if ("followed_by" %in% names(relationships)) relationships else
  mutate(relationships, followed_by = NA_character_)

tibble(
  follows_checked = nrow(checked),
  follow_back = sum(!is.na(checked$followed_by)),
  share_follow_back = mean(!is.na(checked$followed_by)),
  found_by_intersection = length(mutuals)
)
```

Compare `follow_back` with `found_by_intersection`. The direct check
measures reciprocity for the Times's follows exactly, with no sampling,
while the intersection could only see the few mutuals who happened to
follow recently. The general lesson for the rest of the series: when a
question is about *pairs* of accounts, look for an endpoint that answers
it about those pairs, instead of reconstructing it from two lists you
could only partly collect. Kwak et al. (2010) asked whether Twitter was
"a social network or a news media" largely on reciprocity rates like
these; a newsroom that follows a small set of accounts, mostly its own
journalists, and is followed by over a million readers sits near the
"news media" end by construction. Part 03 scales the question up to
whole neighborhoods.

## Ethics and limitations

We teach the mechanics and the ethics in the same document because they
are the same activity: every loop you write collects traces of *people*.
Bluesky's openness (no API keys, no paywall, the whole firehose public
by protocol design) makes collection astonishingly easy, and that ease is
precisely why the judgment has to come from you.

### Public is not the same as consented

Everything we collected is public: anyone with a browser could read it.
It does not follow that the people who posted it agreed to be research
subjects. Fiesler & Proferes (2018) surveyed Twitter users and found
that most had no idea their tweets were used in research, and many were
uncomfortable once they learned, with comfort varying by context: what
topic, which study, whether they would be quoted or named. Most Bluesky
users have never read the AT Protocol documentation and may not realize
that their follows, likes and even *blocks* are globally readable. "It
was public" is where the ethical analysis starts, not where it ends. The
[AoIR Internet Research Ethics guidelines](https://aoir.org/reports/ethics3.pdf)
(franzke et al. 2020), written for researchers without legal training,
frame the right question as one of *contextual* expectations: what flows
of their information would the people in your dataset reasonably
anticipate?

This document's design reflects that: we collected a large
*institutional* account, a newsroom whose public posting is its
professional output, rather than pointing a new loop at a stranger.

### Minimization, third parties, and what you choose not to collect

The cheapest privacy protection is data you never collect. Our flatten
step in Section 5 quietly does ethics: of the dozens of fields in each
response, we kept roughly ten that our questions need. **Purpose
limitation** is the same principle over time: an archive collected to
study posting rhythms should not be quietly repurposed into a profiling
tool. Minimization also has a *who* dimension: our follower archive
holds a couple of thousand accounts that never interacted with this
tutorial, swept in because they once followed the seed, which is why we
capped that sample rather than collecting all of the more than a
million. Prefer aggregates when reporting (the reciprocity share exposes
no individual), and think hard before publishing raw lists of accounts.

### Deletion, withdrawal, and the life of an archive

People delete posts, and deletion is meaningful: it often signals regret,
or that content attracted harassment. The live API honors deletions;
your RDS file does not. Best practice is layered: record the collection
date (our metadata file does); re-check against the live API before
quoting or republishing anything; and share bare post URIs for
re-hydration rather than full content. Verbatim quotation deserves
special caution: a quoted post is trivially re-identifiable with a
search box, even if you "anonymized" the handle (Zimmer 2010), so
paraphrase or aggregate.

### Terms of service, IRBs, and the post-API backdrop

Working through official APIs and their
[rate limits](https://bsky.network/docs/advanced-guides/rate-limits)
keeps you inside the platform's
[terms of service](https://bsky.social/about/support/tos). That is not a
given historically: Freelon (2018) chronicles how Twitter's and
Facebook's API closures stranded a research field and tempted
researchers toward terms-violating scraping. Design your pipeline so its
access method is one you could defend in public. If your work involves
human subjects, talk to your IRB or ethics board *before* collecting:
"public data" does not automatically mean exempt, and boards increasingly
expect a data management plan covering storage, retention,
de-identification and deletion (the metadata file is the first piece of
one).

### Limitations of what we built

Bluesky's users are early adopters and Twitter migrants, not a sample of
any general population, so prevalence claims do not generalize
off-platform, just as Twitter's never did (Ruths & Pfeffer 2014).
Engagement counts condition on visible reactions: the protocol exposes
no impression or view data. A single account's activity supports claims
about that account, and our posts are only its most recent months. The
author feed omits deleted and moderated posts, and engagement counters
are point-in-time snapshots that keep changing after collection. And the
platform is in flux: lexicons, limits and moderation infrastructure
evolve, which is why we save snapshots, record parameters, and treat
re-collection as a new measurement rather than a refresh.

## Exercises

These extend the document in roughly increasing order of ambition. For
any exercise that collects new data, write down the sampling frame and
estimate the request budget *before* running anything.

1. **Collect a different account.** Repoint the pipeline at the official
   [`bsky.app`](https://bsky.app/profile/bsky.app) account. Start from
   `bs_get_profile()` to size the job: its follower count is in the
   millions, so cap followers at a small `limit` (say 2,000) and record
   the truncation honestly in your metadata file.
2. **Change the page size and time it.** With `limit > 100` bskyr asks
   for 100 per request, so loop over cursors yourself with
   `bs_get_author_feed(HANDLE, limit = 25, cursor = ...)` for the same
   number of posts, wrapping each approach in `system.time()`. How do
   the request count and wall-clock time change? This is why you should
   usually ask for the largest page an endpoint allows.
3. **Explore the `filter` parameter.** The
   [`getAuthorFeed`](https://endpoints.bsky.app/#bluesky-app/tag/appbskyfeed/GET/xrpc/app.bsky.feed.getAuthorFeed)
   endpoint accepts `filter` values such as `posts_no_replies` and
   `posts_with_media`. bskyr's function has no `filter` argument, so send
   the request with httr2 (as Section 4 did for the rate-limit headers,
   against `https://public.api.bsky.app/xrpc/app.bsky.feed.getAuthorFeed`).
   Compare the media-only feed's size to the `has_embed` share from
   Section 7. They won't match, because embeds include link cards and
   quoted posts as well as images; explaining the gap is the exercise.
4. **CSV vs. RDS vs. Parquet at different scales.** Slice the post
   archive to its first 100, 500, 1,000 and all rows; write each slice
   as CSV, RDS and (with the [arrow](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/r/)
   package) Parquet; and plot file size and load time against row count.
   Does each binary format's advantage grow, shrink or hold steady?
5. **A polite multi-account crawler.** Sample five accounts from
   `follows` and collect each one's most recent ~200 posts, pausing
   between accounts and saving one RDS file per account plus a single
   shared metadata JSON. Estimate the total request budget first, then
   confirm afterward that the actual count matched.
6. **Watch backoff work, without hammering the server.** Write a fake
   function that signals an error of class `httr2_http_429` (use
   `rlang::abort("RateLimitExceeded", class = "httr2_http_429")`) on its
   first two calls and succeeds on the third, then pass it to
   `call_with_backoff()`. You should see two retry messages and then a
   result. Try a fake that fails with a different error too: it should
   fail at once, without retrying.

## Research project ideas

Three research designs that need nothing beyond this document's
endpoints and methods, each sketched as *question → data → method →
expected challenge*.

**1. The migration cohorts of Bluesky.** Did users who arrived during the
post-US-election surge of late 2024 behave differently from earlier
adopters, and did they stay? The follower sample carries each account's
creation date (hydrate it with `bs_get_profile()`), so you can define
joining cohorts directly. Sample a few dozen accounts per cohort, collect
their posting histories, and compare activity: posts per month since
joining, time to last post, share still active. The challenge is the
sampling frame (Ruths & Pfeffer 2014): the most recent followers of one
newsroom are not Bluesky users in general, and deleted and suspended
accounts have *already* vanished from follower lists, which biases
retention estimates upward.

**2. A social network or a news media?** Kwak et al. (2010) found that
only about 22% of Twitter follow relationships were reciprocated. Is
Bluesky different? Choose a defensible frame (for instance, all members
of a few public starter packs spanning different communities), collect
each account's follows (capping very large accounts and recording the
caps), and compute per-account reciprocity with
`bs_get_relationships()`, as in Section 7, rather than by intersecting
two capped lists. Compare reciprocity across community types and
account size. The challenge is scale and politeness: this is the project
where request budgeting, backoff and overnight pacing become method.

**3. How fast do archives decay?** Your RDS file is a snapshot of a
moving target. Take today's post URIs, then once a week re-hydrate a
fixed random sample with [`bs_get_posts()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_posts.html)
and record which no longer resolve. After a couple of months, estimate a
deletion rate and ask what kinds of posts disappear: replies?
high-engagement posts? particular topics? This design sits directly on
the ethics literature (Fiesler & Proferes 2018): the deletion-respecting
practices above become your *findings*. The challenge is interpretive:
you observe that a post vanished, not why.
